> this is expected and desired behavior. that's what loading is there for.

Then is there any way I'm missing to store a reference to a scene/resource without actually loading all of its textures into VRAM? How do you handle having a large set of resources each of them with a couple of textures/scenes assigned?

I don't think loading into VRAM every texture that has a reference is a scalable approach. You either avoid using direct references, which goes against Godot's own design, or ignore the big impact that can have on memory in games with a lot of content.

Not just texture, the engine loads all dependencies of a packed scene. Also, `ResourceLoader.load(path, "PackedScene", ResourceLoader.CACHE_MODE_IGNORE_DEEP)` is misleading (https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/59669). It doesn't store to the cache but it loads all dependencies anyway.. There is no workaround besides manually loading with string paths only right before instantiating.

This is a pretty big problem. I was under the impression that storing `PackedScene`s in an `[Export]` variable can be used to avoid loading the scene until you instantiate it, but all of the textures are loaded anyway, making `PackedScene` essentially useless.

Edit:
My current workaround is to use an `[Export]` variable for the scene's file path instead:
```cs
[Export(PropertyHint.File)] public string MyScenePath { get; private set; }
```

> Face same problem and also rewrite logic to handle path BUT after loading scene and queuing it free after some time textures still in VRAM.

I think this may be because the `PackedScene` resource is cached.

You can avoid the cache entirely:
```cs
ResourceLoader.Load<PackedScene>("a/b/c.tcsn", cacheMode: ResourceLoader.CacheMode.Ignore)
```

Setting CacheMode did nothing in my case.
Turns out that this memory leak is not actually leak. Just system resources pressure wasn't enough to auto trigger garbage collection.

I have added manual garbage collection after scene changing background node

```csharp
        GC.Collect(GC.MaxGeneration);
        GC.WaitForPendingFinalizers();
```

So now changing scene background explicitly clears all dangling resources including expired tweens.

I think this is not necessary in most cases but may be important for those who target smallest possible memory usage.
And may be useful to manually trigger GC in specific moments to reduce fps stutters in more critical moments.

I did the same. **Saving resources as filepaths and loading them when needed is the way to go for now.** So if you're reading this looking for a solution, just replace your explicit resource variables with `@export_file(...) var my_resource: String` and load them when needed with `ResourceLoader.load(my_resource)`.

However, that is not ideal since:
- Filepaths don't have the Quick Load menu available, so you have to manually search for each resource to assign it. For small jam projects, this is okay; for bigger commercial ones, this is not.
- Filepaths cannot enforce the type of the resource, you can only set a filter and hope for the best.
- Filepaths are more limited in how they can be stored. For example you cannot do `Dictionary[StringName, String]` and have the values of the dictionary behave as filepaths in the editor. For this you'd have to add more indirection building your own resource to store one filepath, e.g. `Dictionary[StringName, CustomFilepath]`, or to store each pair `Array[CustomNamedResource]`.
- Filepaths don't change when files are moved. Since most of them will use UIDs, this is more of an edge case, but it can still break things for some people.

I think the simplest way to solve this would be to improve filepath support in the editor, making it behave more like resources themselves to mitigate these issues. Maybe having a `Filepath` or `ResourceRef` native resource that automatically handles this would a better way to do this without having to rely on export flags, which can be limiting, although I don't know if the overhead of a resource is worth it for such a small task. Ideally it would allow a syntax like `Filepath[MyResourceType]` to enforce the type of the referenced file from code, though I have no idea how hard that would be to implement.

In any case, I think it's mandatory to explain in the documentation that when storing a reference to a resource, you are actually loading it (and all of its references, recursively) into memory. I couldn't find anywhere where this is stated explicitly, but maybe I missed something.

I'm closing this because I don't think the original complaint makes much sense. Obviously if you reference a thing, the thing has to be loaded into memory so it's ready when you use the variable.

I'll make a proposal to improve filepath support in the editor, which is the actual issue here.
